pages.text: Watch: Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip Skip to content Site search Home News Sport Business Technology Health Culture Arts Travel Earth Audio Video Live Documentaries Weather Newsletters Watch Live Pope Leo rides in helicopter cockpit during Peru trip Pope Leo XIV shared a cockpit with pilots from the Peruvian Air Force during his tour of Latin America. Sharing the video to social media, the force said having the Pope join its pilots on Saturday was "an honour and an unforgettable memory". On Sunday, the pontiff arrived in Cusco, a southern Andes Mountains city that was once the heart of the Inca empire. There, the Pope visited an ancient Inca fortress, where he said religious traditions could help counter an age marked by "divisions, wounds, mistrust," stressing that faith should unite people and bring them together "in the light of faith and love." The Peruvian leg of his tour holds special significance for the Pope. He not only lived in Peru for long periods between 1985 and 2023 but also became a citizen of the country in 2015, forging close ties with local communities. pages.text: We’ve Been Strapping Cargo to Our Backs for Millions of Years, but Backpack Innovation Really Took Off Around the Civil War Skip to main content Illustration by Emily Lankiewicz / Images via public domain Humans have been carting things on our backs in wraps of some kind at least since we began using tools, around two million years ago—and we have always sought ways to make the load more comfortable. The oldest known backpack ever discovered, in the Alps on the border between Austria and Italy, employed two narrow wooden boards and a hazel rod for a frame. The contraption dates to around 3300 B.C. and is credited to Ötzi the Iceman , a glacier mummy unearthed alongside it in 1991. But what we recognize as a backpack is much newer. In 1865, Henry Clay Merriam led a regiment of Black Union troops in an attack against Fort Blakely, a Confederate stronghold in Alabama. His deeds in this final battle of the Civil War earned him a Medal of Honor “for conspicuous gallantry.” Afterward, the lieutenant colonel had an epiphany: It was burdensome to carry both a knapsack (a pack with shoulder straps but no frame for internal support) and a haversack (a shoulder bag containing his rations). Based on his time carrying gear for the Army, Merriam devised a solution: a boxy canvas pack with room for socks, a quart of water, a shaving kit and a deck of cards, plus a compartment for rations in a case at the bottom. In the biomedical research community, medical imaging phantoms are objects used as stand-ins for human tissues to ensure that systems and methods for imaging the human body are operating correctly. In Pursuit of the Answer, Astronauts Have Been Making a Home in Microgravity for Decades Skip to main content The entrance to "At Home in Space" at the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum Daniel Soñé / National Air and Space Museum Imagine waking up in a zippered sleeping bag 250 miles above the ground, contained in a vessel traveling five miles per second in a permanent state of free-fall . Each day includes about two hours of exercise to stave off the atrophy of your bones and muscles. And to get home, you must blast through Earth’s atmosphere in a spacecraft. This is life on the International Space Station, where groups of humans have lived and worked continuously for nearly 26 years . “It’s very risky, but there’s a reason we do it,” says Jennifer Levasseur , a curator at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum. Acid rain, or acid deposition, is a broad term that includes any form of precipitation with acidic components, such as sulfuric or nitric acid that fall to the ground from the atmosphere in wet or dry forms. This can include rain, snow, fog, hail or even dust that is acidic. What Causes Acid Rain? This image illustrates the pathway for acid rain in our environment: (1) Emissions of SO2 and NOx are released into the air, where (2) the pollutants are transformed into acid particles that may be transported long distances. (3) These acid particles then fall to the earth as wet and dry deposition (dust, rain, snow, etc.) and (4) may cause harmful effects on soil, forests, streams, and lakes. Acid rain results when sulfur dioxide (SO 2 ) and nitrogen oxides (NO X ) are emitted into the atmosphere and transported by wind and air currents. The SO 2 and NO X react with water, oxygen and other chemicals to form sulfuric and nitric acids. These then mix with water and other materials before falling to the ground. The Macedonian general, probable bigamist , and body snatcher turned self-styled pharaoh wanted to make Alexandria the intellectual capital of the world. Having intercepted the corpse of Alexander the Great on its way home to Macedonia, he instead interred it in Alexandria to legitimize his rule. LIFE, BESIEGED Most of the animals shown here are among the more than 28,000 species of animals and plants that the International Union for Conservation of Nature says are threatened with extinction. That number actually understates the risk. Since 1964, when the IUCN established a “ red list ” of threatened species and began compiling data gathered worldwide, the list has become the preeminent global database of endangered life and an essential tool for conservation policy. Yet the IUCN has been able to assess only about 106,000 species of the more than 1.5 million species of animals and more than 300,000 plants that scientists have described and named—which they estimate is less than a quarter of what’s really out there. A recent intergovernmental report on the biodiversity crisis estimated that extinction threatens up to a million animal and plant species, known and unknown. The IUCN hopes to raise the number of species assessments to 160,000 by 2020. Next up on its agenda: a “ green list ” of conservation successes. It will be much shorter than the red one.
